A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Fission-GRPO work. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across revisions and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original BFCL experiments across three Qwen3 sizes, feedback ablations, trigger-frequency sensitivity results, and a qualitative recovery case study.

after.justification: v2 retains those results and adds TAU-Bench and TAU2-Bench evaluations, automated and human simulator assessments, matched-update comparisons, and training curves.

M1.justification: The three-stage framework and Error Simulator architecture remain. Section 3.2 revises the reported reward design: the maximum format contribution decays from 3 to 2 instead of 2 to 1, aggregation explicitly divides by three, and the length penalty is recast as a positive compliance reward. Whether these revisions reflect implementation changes or corrections to its description is not established.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates on BFCL alone. v2 adds TAU-Bench Retail/Airline and TAU2-Bench Retail/Airline/Telecom, introducing simulated-user interactions and different tool environments. Section 4.5 also evaluates simulator failures from unseen e-commerce order-management and calendar-scheduling domains. The original training-domain coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds AWPO as an evaluated comparator at Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, including on the retained BFCL benchmark. The existing Base, GRPO, DAPO, Dr.GRPO, ToolACE-2-8B, and BitAgent-8B comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 introduces pass@1 evaluation with GLM-5 simulated users, simulator judging on 200 in-domain and 200 out-of-domain failures, a 100-output human assessment, and comparisons matching 312 or 432 updates with G'=G. The trigger study's stated budget also changes from 234 total global steps to 234 standard updates; the PDFs do not establish that its retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: The original feedback ablation, trigger sensitivity study, and recovery case remain. v2 adds simulator generalization and leakage assessments in Section 4.5, controls testing whether additional updates explain gains in Section 4.6, and training-stability analysis through reward curves in Appendix B.

E5.justification: v2 first reports inter-annotator agreement: Cohen's kappa of 0.71 for two annotators assessing 100 simulator outputs. Both versions mention multiple runs for threshold selection, but neither specifies training-run counts, seeds, or benchmark confidence intervals. Increased repeated training is not established.

E6.justification: Existing BFCL scores, feedback-ablation values, and original plotted results remain unchanged. v2 adds extensive TAU results, simulator-quality findings, and matched-update accuracies: Fission-GRPO versus GRPO scores 46.75 versus 41.75 at 432 updates and 46.12 versus 43.75 at 312 updates. Added AWPO results also change the Missing Parameter leaders at 4B and 8B.

T1.justification: v2 explicitly defines the normalized composite reward, corrects the stated functional-reward range from [0,2] to [0,1], and replaces the gradient expression labeled as an objective in Equation 6 with a clipped-ratio/KL surrogate consistent with the existing pseudocode. These are limited mathematical corrections; no theorems or proofs are added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand the empirical contribution from BFCL robustness to generalization across TAU-Bench and TAU2-Bench, claiming leading results across most settings and gains up to 17.4 percentage points. The original fission contribution and headline BFCL gains remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive arguments separating fission benefits from teacher-provided feedback information and additional update counts, interprets simulator generalization and leakage assessments, and argues that training remains stable. The limitations now identify tool-calling as the evaluation boundary rather than BFCL alone and discuss costs at larger model scales or with expensive APIs.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code repository link and discloses alpha=0.5. Algorithm 1 is reconciled with the main text concerning ground-truth simulator input, deduplication by context and failed call, and composite-reward computation. The first two details already appeared in v1's prose. Hardware, principal training hyperparameters, and simulator prompt templates remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for TAU-Bench, TAU2-Bench, AWPO, Silver and Sutton's experience-based learning perspective, and several online/deep-research agent works. These broaden the motivation and neighboring literature while retaining the central positioning against offline error corpora and existing GRPO variants.

P1.justification: Existing passages are substantially rewritten or condensed across the abstract, introduction, both related-work subsections, main results, feedback discussion, and limitations. Main-result subheadings are consolidated, the experimental narrative is reorganized, and a training-curve appendix is inserted before the retained algorithm and case-study appendices.

P2.justification: Table 1 is redesigned with model-group headers and three benchmark column groups; Tables 3–4 and training Figure 5 are added. Figures 1b and 3 are redrawn, with Figure 3 changing from horizontal to vertical panels. Table highlighting and placement change, while the simulator prompts and case visualization are retained as Figures 6–7.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked evaluation beyond BFCL and direct simulator-quality or matched-update checks. v2 substantially addresses these gaps through broader interactive benchmarks, automated and human simulator assessments, and update-matched controls in Tables 1, 3, and 4. Corrected equations and pseudocode further improve clarity. Benchmark uncertainty and total simulator costs remain insufficiently quantified, but the added evidence materially strengthens the paper.
